title: Apartment and High-Rise Emergency Preparedness
summary: How to prepare an apartment or high-rise home for outages, fires, and floods when elevators, water pumps, and building staff may not work. Do this before anything goes wrong.

steps.title: Survey your building now
steps.body: Spend 30 minutes walking your building on a normal day. Find every exit stairwell on your floor, not just the closest one - the nearest stair may be blocked by smoke. Count the flights from your floor to the street and note which doors lead outside versus into a garage or courtyard. Find the fire alarm pull stations, extinguishers, and the outside meeting place. Ask management four questions: Is the building sprinklered? Is it fire-resistive ('fireproof') or not? What does the backup generator run (lights, one elevator, water pumps, fire pumps)? How will they send emergency notices (intercom, text, email)? In New York, building type is often posted in the lobby. Write the answers on one page and keep it with your go-bag.

steps.title: Learn the stairwells in the dark
steps.body: Walk down your main stairwell once with only a headlamp and your go-bag so you know how long it takes and how tired you get. Count doors as you go - in smoke you may not be able to read floor signs. Keep stairwell doors closed; they are fire doors and must self-close. Report blocked exits, missing exit lights, or piled trash to management, as fire officials advise. If anyone in your home uses a wheelchair, cannot hear alarms, or cannot manage many flights, tell building management now and build a personal evacuation plan with a support network. Building staff must evacuate too and may not be able to reach every resident.

steps.title: Plan for no elevators and no water pressure
steps.body: In a power outage, elevators stop unless they are on generator power, and many owners keep only one running. Buildings taller than about six stories usually need electric pumps to push water to upper floors. When the pumps stop, taps on high floors can run dry within hours. When an outage is forecast or starts, fill clean containers, pots, and a bathtub (for flushing and washing) right away. Store at least 1 gallon (about 3.8 L) of drinking water per person per day for several days. Know the hidden water already in your unit - see the urban water guide. Plan how you will carry water and groceries up the stairs, and check on neighbors who cannot.

steps.title: Decide: stay in place or leave
steps.body: Staying home is usually safer than moving into crowded streets, but some threats override that. Leave at once if there is fire in your own unit, you smell gas, the building is visibly damaged, or officials order an evacuation. For a fire elsewhere in the building, follow announcements and fire department instructions - in fire-resistive buildings the FDNY often advises staying in your sealed unit rather than entering smoke-filled halls (see the high-rise fire guide). For flooding, move up, never down into basements or garages. For street-level unrest or chemical releases, stay inside above it. Recheck your decision every 30-60 minutes as news comes in.

steps.title: Stock the unit for 2 weeks
steps.body: Apartments are small, so store smart. Keep at least a 3-day kit ready and work toward 2 weeks of water, food that needs no cooking, medicines, and lighting. Use battery or rechargeable LED lights, not candles - a candle fire in a tower puts everyone at risk. Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors or on a balcony; carbon monoxide can drift into your unit or a neighbor's. Charge power banks when an outage is forecast. Keep a bucket-toilet kit (heavy bags, lid, kitty litter) in case drains back up or water stops. Store cash in small bills, since card readers fail without power.

steps.title: Manage e-bike and scooter batteries
steps.body: Lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes and scooters have caused many deadly apartment fires in big cities. In 2025 the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission advanced a proposed safety standard for these batteries after many fatal fires. Until it is final, charge only with the original or a certified compatible charger, never charge a battery that is hot or damaged, and do not charge while you sleep or are away. Keep the bike and charger away from your apartment door so a fire cannot block your only exit. Never open a pack or swap cells. If a battery hisses, smokes, or swells, get out, close the door, and call 911.

steps.title: Build a floor network
steps.body: Meet the neighbors on your floor before an emergency. Trade phone numbers, find out who is older, has a disability, uses home oxygen or other powered medical equipment, or has small kids, and agree to knock on each other's doors in an outage or alarm. One trusted neighbor can watch your unit, share water, or help carry someone down stairs. Keep your household plan simple: two meeting places (one just outside the building, one outside the neighborhood) and an out-of-area contact everyone texts. Keep lights shaded and voices low in a long grid-down event, but do not hide from the neighbors who can help you.

warnings: Never use an elevator during a fire or when the fire alarm is sounding unless the fire department tells you to.
Never prop open stairwell or apartment fire doors - an open door lets smoke and heat race through halls and stairs.
Never use a grill, camp stove, or generator inside or on a balcony - carbon monoxide can kill you and your neighbors.
Do not move down into a basement or garage during flooding - water and electrical hazards collect there first.
proTips: Keep a headlamp and shoes by your bed - most fires and outages that kill people start at night.
Fill water containers the moment an outage is forecast; upper-floor taps may stop before the lights do.
Ask management to text outage and alarm notices; a building text list beats knocking on 200 doors.
Photograph the evacuation map posted in your hallway so you have it on your phone.
source: NFPA / USFA / FDNY / NYC HPD / CPSC

sources.title: State Fire Marshal Offers Safety Tips for High-Rise Dwellers (NFPA guidance)
Emergency Planning and Evacuations Guide
sources.publisher: NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development

whenNotTo: Do not wait in place to 'shelter' when the fire is in your own unit, you smell gas, or officials order evacuation - leave.

quickGlance.situation: You live above the ground floor and an outage, fire alarm, or storm is coming or has started.
immediate: Fill water containers now before upper-floor pumps stop
Put shoes, headlamp, keys, and phone by the door
Know two stairwells from your floor and never use the elevator in a fire
then: Check on floor neighbors who are older, disabled, or on powered medical devices
Follow building announcements and recheck your stay-or-go decision every 30-60 minutes

title: City Water Outage - Finding and Storing Urban Water
summary: Where to find safe water in an apartment or city home when the taps stop, how to get it out safely, and which city water sources you should never drink.

steps.title: Fill containers the moment trouble starts
steps.body: City water often keeps flowing for a while after a main break, pump failure, or power outage, then pressure drops - fastest on upper floors of tall buildings that rely on electric booster pumps. As soon as an outage starts or is forecast, fill clean food-grade jugs, pots, and pitchers with drinking water. Fill the bathtub too, but use tub water for flushing and washing unless you used a clean food-grade tub liner. Aim for at least 1 gallon (about 3.8 L) per person per day for drinking and basic hygiene, and more for hot weather, nursing mothers, and sick people. Label containers with the date. Do not use containers that ever held chemicals, fuel, or cleaners.

steps.title: Drain the water heater safely
steps.body: A tank water heater holds 30-80 gallons (115-300 L) of water that was safe when it entered your home. Use only the heater that feeds your faucets and shower, not a boiler for radiator heat. First turn off the power at the breaker (electric) or set the gas valve to 'pilot' or 'off' (gas). Running an empty heater can damage it or start a fire. Close the cold-water inlet valve on top, open a hot tap somewhere in the home to let air in, then open the drain valve at the bottom into a clean container. Let the water cool - it may be scalding. The first water out may have sediment; let it settle or filter it. Refill the tank fully before turning the heater back on.

steps.title: Use the water in your pipes, ice, and toilet tank
steps.body: Water sitting in your pipes is usable. Open a faucet at the highest point of your home to let in air, then collect water from the lowest faucet. Melted ice cubes are fine if they were made with safe water. The toilet tank (the box behind the seat, never the bowl) holds 1-3 gallons, but use it for drinking only if the water is clear and no blue or color-changing cleaner was ever added; otherwise use it for flushing. Liquid from canned fruits and vegetables also counts as fluid. If officials say the city water may be contaminated, shut your main water valve so bad water does not flow into your pipes and water heater.

steps.title: Know which city sources are not safe
steps.body: Pool and hot-tub water is for washing and flushing only, never drinking. Fountains, ponds, retention basins, and rivers in a city can carry sewage, fuel, road runoff, and chemicals. Floodwater is especially dangerous. The CDC is clear that water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or household disinfection, so do not drink it or bathe in it. If water smells like fuel or chemicals, looks oily, or is dark with solids, skip it. Do not open fire hydrants - it is illegal in most cities, drops pressure firefighters need, and the force can injure you.

steps.title: Treat any water you are unsure of
steps.body: When a boil-water notice is issued, or you are using rainwater or another outside source that is not chemically contaminated, treat it before drinking, brushing teeth, or making baby formula. Let cloudy water settle, then pour off or filter the clear water through a clean cloth. Bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 feet or about 2,000 m). If you cannot boil, use plain unscented household bleach following the label or the water disinfection guides in this app, or a filter rated for bacteria and protozoa. Follow your water utility's notices - they tell you when tap water is safe again and whether to flush your pipes.

steps.title: Find official water distribution
steps.body: In long outages, cities and relief groups set up water distribution points, often at fire stations, schools, or parks. Listen to local radio, check official city and utility social media, or call or text 211 for locations. Bring your own clean containers and a cart or wagon - water weighs about 8.3 pounds per gallon (1 kg per liter), and you may be carrying it up many flights. Red Cross shelters and service sites also provide water. Hotels, hospitals, and big commercial buildings sometimes have their own storage, but do not count on them sharing it.

steps.title: Store water before the next outage
steps.body: Apartment storage works best in many small containers that fit under beds and in closets. Commercial bottled water keeps until the date on the label. If you fill your own food-grade containers with tap water, replace it about every 6 months. Keep stored water away from sunlight, heat, and chemicals. A 2-week supply for one person is about 14 gallons (53 L). Check your floor's load limits before putting large drums on a balcony - a full 55-gallon drum weighs over 450 pounds (205 kg). Rain barrels can supply flushing and garden water, but treat rainwater before drinking.

warnings: Turn off the power or gas to a water heater before draining it, and refill it completely before turning it back on.
Water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe at home - do not drink, cook with, or bathe in it.
Never drink toilet-tank water that has a blue or colored cleaner in it, and never use bowl water.
Do not open fire hydrants - it can injure you and steals pressure firefighters need.
proTips: Fill the bathtub for flushing; one bucket poured fast into the bowl flushes most toilets.
Put a small sticky note on the water heater showing where the drain valve and cold-water shutoff are.
A folding hand truck or wagon makes carrying water up stairs possible for one person.
Freeze a few jugs of water; they keep a fridge cold in an outage and become drinking water as they melt.

sources.title: How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: Emergency Planning and Evacuations Guide
sources.publisher: NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development

whenNotTo: Do not use any tap, pipe, or water heater water if officials say the city supply has chemical contamination - use bottled or delivered water.
Do not drain a water heater while it is still powered or the gas is on.

quickGlance.situation: City water has stopped or is about to stop, or a boil-water notice has been issued.
immediate: Fill clean jugs and pots now, and the tub for flushing
Turn off power or gas before draining the water heater
Use only clear toilet-tank water with no blue cleaner
then: Boil or disinfect any water you are unsure of
Call or text 211 or check official channels for water distribution points

title: Civil Disturbance - Shelter in Place Protocol
summary: How to stay safe at home or work when protests turn violent or rioting breaks out nearby: stay away, stay inside, stay informed, and know the conditions that mean you must leave.

steps.title: Find out where the trouble is
steps.body: Civil disturbances are usually limited to certain streets or districts and can move quickly. Before you decide anything, figure out where the activity is relative to you and which way it is heading. Use more than one source: local TV or radio, your city or county alert system, official police and emergency management social media, and a battery or crank NOAA weather radio. Neighborhood apps can be fast but are often wrong - confirm with an official source. If the trouble is not on your block, the safest move is usually to stay where you are and keep away from the area entirely.

steps.title: Get inside, lock up, stay away from windows
steps.body: Emergency managers give the same core advice: stay away from the area, lock your doors, and stay clear of windows. Bring everyone inside, including pets. Close blinds and curtains so people outside cannot see in and so broken glass is less likely to hit you. Move to an inner room or hallway if you hear breaking glass, gunfire, or explosions nearby. Park cars in a garage if you can do it without driving toward the disturbance. Do not go outside to watch, film, or 'check it out' - curiosity puts people in the wrong place when police move a crowd or when violence starts.

steps.title: Keep a low profile
steps.body: A brightly lit home with people at the windows draws attention when the street is dark and tense. Keep lights dim and away from windows, and do not stand silhouetted in front of them. Keep voices and TV volume low; use earbuds for news. Do not post your address, your supplies, or live video from your window on social media. Do not shout at, threaten, or argue with people outside. Confrontation turns a crowd passing by into a crowd focused on you. The goal is for your building to look like every other quiet building on the block.

steps.title: Harden doors and windows without trapping yourself
steps.body: Lock every door and window. A door security bar or wedge braces a door against kicks better than the lock alone. Put a dowel or bar in the track of sliding doors so they cannot be forced open. Close and lock ground-floor windows and move valuables out of sight. Do not nail shut or block doors and windows you may need to escape through - fire is a real risk during riots, and you must be able to get out fast. Keep the path to at least two exits clear. Have your go-bag, shoes, keys, phone, and medicines by the door.

steps.title: Know when to leave
steps.body: Staying put is the default, but leave right away if: smoke or fire threatens your building, police or emergency managers order you out, you smell gas, the building is damaged, or violence enters your building. Leave by the exit farthest from the crowd, move away from the noise, and do not go toward police lines from behind the crowd. Walk, do not run, unless you are in immediate danger. Have a destination picked ahead of time - a friend's home in another part of town, a hotel, or an official shelter. If you drive and a crowd surrounds your car, keep doors locked, stay calm, and drive slowly away when a path opens.

steps.title: Follow police instructions and report danger
steps.body: When police or the National Guard arrive, listen to and follow their directions, including curfews. Curfew orders apply to you even if you are only walking to a store. If you must be out, carry ID and be ready to explain where you are going. If the situation escalates and you see violence, fire, or people in danger, call 911 and report what you see and the exact location. Use text messages to reach family - texts get through more often than calls when networks are busy. Pick one out-of-area contact everyone checks in with.

steps.title: After it calms down
steps.body: Make sure the area is truly safe before you go outside - check official sources, not just the quiet street. Watch for broken glass, burned structures that may collapse, downed power lines, and leftover debris. Photograph any damage to your property and report it to police and your insurer. Check on neighbors, especially older people living alone. Talk to someone if you feel shaken; fear, poor sleep, and jumpiness are normal after a frightening night and usually fade. Seek mental health support if they do not.

warnings: Never confront, threaten, or argue with people outside - that is how a passing crowd becomes a crowd at your door.
Do not block or nail shut every exit - fire is common during riots and you must be able to get out.
Defending property with force carries serious legal risk; know your state's laws, and remember property can be replaced and people cannot.
Do not go out to watch or film - bystanders get hurt by crowd surges, chemical agents, and violence.
proTips: A simple rule: hear it - stay in and tune in; see it - move away from windows; it is in your building - leave by the far exit.
Keep a small amount of cash in small bills; card readers and ATMs may be closed.
Sign up for your county's alert system now so warnings reach your phone without searching.
Keep curtains closed as a habit in tense times so nothing changes when trouble starts.

sources.title: Civil Disorder
sources.publisher: Fairfax County Department of Emergency Management and Security

whenNotTo: Do not stay in place if fire, smoke, gas, structural damage, or an evacuation order threatens your building - leave by the safest exit.
Do not try to shelter in a car stuck in or near a crowd if you can safely drive or walk away from it.

quickGlance.situation: A protest has turned violent or rioting is happening near your home or workplace.
immediate: Stay away from the area and get everyone inside
Lock doors and stay clear of windows
Tune to official news and alerts
then: Leave by the far exit if fire, gas, damage, an order, or violence reaches your building
Follow police directions and curfews; call 911 to report danger

title: Urban Navigation Without Power
summary: How to find your way across a dark city when phones die, signals are out, and street signs are hard to see - using the street grid, paper maps, landmarks, and careful movement at dead intersections.

steps.title: Learn your city's street grid
steps.body: Most U.S. cities follow a pattern you can learn in an afternoon. Find out where the zero lines are - the two streets where address numbering starts - and which way numbers rise. In many cities numbered streets run one direction and named or numbered avenues cross them. Once you know the pattern, any address tells you roughly how far and which way to go. Learn how many blocks equal a mile in your area; in many grids it is 8 to 12 short blocks or 4 to 6 long ones. Walk your neighborhood and note how the pattern bends near rivers, rail lines, and highways, where grids often break.

steps.title: Carry a paper map and offline maps
steps.body: Digital maps need battery, and cell data may be down. Keep a paper street map of your city in your get-home bag, and mark your home, work, schools, bridges, hospitals, and two meeting places on it. Free transit system maps often show streets well enough for walking. Download offline map areas on your phone before an emergency. Your phone's GPS chip works without cell service as long as it has battery, so an offline map plus GPS still shows your position. Turn on low-power mode, dim the screen, and check the map only at decision points to save battery.

steps.title: Use landmarks and dead reckoning
steps.body: Pick 2-3 big landmarks in each direction from home - a tall tower, a stadium, a river, a hill - that you can see from far away. When you lose track, find one and reorient. For dead reckoning, start at a known point, note your direction, and count blocks as you go. At every turn, say out loud where you think you are ('6 blocks north, now heading east on Main'). A compass or the sun helps: in the U.S. the sun is in the southern part of the sky at midday. If what you see does not match what you expect, stop and figure it out before you walk farther in the wrong direction.

steps.title: Cross dark intersections safely
steps.body: When traffic signals are dark, drivers are supposed to treat the intersection as an all-way stop: stop fully, then yield to the car on the right, and take turns. Many drivers do not. Crashes rise sharply at dark signals during outages. As a pedestrian, make eye contact with drivers before stepping out, cross with a group if you can, and never assume a car will stop. As a driver, slow well before the intersection, stop fully, and watch for walkers you cannot see. Police may direct traffic at major crossings - their signals override everything else.

steps.title: Avoid bottlenecks
steps.body: In a big emergency, crowds pour onto the main boulevards, bridges, and transit hubs, and those routes jam fast. Use parallel streets one or two blocks over. Know at least three ways across any river or highway between work and home, including pedestrian bridges. Leaving earlier than the crowd usually beats any shortcut. Stay off highways on foot - it is often illegal and very dangerous. Never go into tunnels, underpasses, subway entrances, or culverts during heavy rain or flooding; low spots fill fast and water can hide open manholes.

steps.title: Move at night only when you must
steps.body: A city with no streetlights is far more dangerous at night: holes, debris, downed wires, and drivers who cannot see you. If you can, wait for daylight. If you must move, let your eyes adjust to the dark for 20-30 minutes, then use a headlamp on low or red mode and switch to white light at steps, curbs, and debris. Wear something bright or reflective so drivers see you. Stay on main sidewalks with other people rather than empty alleys or shortcuts. Treat every downed wire as live and stay at least 35 feet (about 10 m) away.

steps.title: Practice the route before you need it
steps.body: Walk at least part of your route from work to home on a nice day. Time it, find rest spots (libraries, fire stations, hospitals, big grocery stores), and note where the route crosses bridges or rail lines. Try one leg with your phone in your pocket and only the paper map. Practice is what makes navigation work when you are tired, stressed, and in the dark.

warnings: Dark traffic signals cause many crashes - never assume a driver will stop for you.
Stay out of tunnels, underpasses, and subway entrances during heavy rain or flooding.
Treat every downed power line as live and stay well away from it.
Do not walk on highways or rail tracks - it is dangerous and usually illegal.
proTips: Write your home address, meeting places, and an out-of-area contact on a card in your wallet.
Mark every bridge and river crossing on your paper map with a highlighter - they are the choke points.
A small button compass on your bag zipper costs little and settles direction arguments fast.
Screenshots of your route maps load instantly with no data and little battery.
source: Boulder Office of Disaster Management / NYC Emergency Management

sources.title: Driving Safely During a Power Outage
Plan Now NYC - make an emergency plan

whenNotTo: Do not set out across the city if officials are telling people to shelter in place, or during a curfew.
Do not move at night if you can safely wait for daylight.

quickGlance.situation: The power is out across the city and you need to get somewhere without reliable phone maps.
immediate: Use your paper map or offline map and confirm your starting point
Treat dark signals as all-way stops and make eye contact before crossing
Pick big landmarks and count blocks as you go
then: Use parallel streets to avoid crowded bridges and boulevards
Wait for daylight if you can; if not, light up and stay on main streets

title: Public Transportation Failure - Getting Home on Foot
summary: A plan for getting home on foot when trains, buses, and roads stop working - from knowing your distance to the first 30 minutes, group travel, and protecting your feet.

steps.title: Know how far home really is
steps.body: Measure the walking distance from work, school, and other regular places to home before you ever need it. Most adults walk 2.5-3 mph (4-5 km/h) on city sidewalks; with a bag, crowds, and rests, plan on about 2 mph (3 km/h). A 10-mile (16 km) walk can take 5 hours or more. With children or older adults, plan slower and with more stops. If home is too far to walk in one day, pick a safe place to stay near work - a friend, coworker, or relative - as NYC Emergency Management advises for commuters who live outside the city. Write these times and fallback places down.

steps.title: Keep a get-home kit at work
steps.body: City emergency managers recommend keeping comfortable walking shoes at your desk and some emergency cash, since ATMs may not work. Add a small bag with water (1 liter or more), a few snack bars, a phone power bank and cable, a paper map with your route marked, a rain layer, a flashlight or headlamp, a dust mask, basic blister supplies, and any daily medicines. Keep it light - under 10 pounds (4.5 kg) - so you will actually carry it. On days with bad weather or big events forecast, wear walking shoes and carry the kit.

steps.title: Plan two routes and rest stops
steps.body: Map a main route home and a backup that uses different bridges and streets. Mark every bridge, tunnel, and rail crossing - they are where crowds jam or police close roads. Note rest stops every 2-3 miles where you can find water, restrooms, and shelter, such as libraries, community centers, large stores, and hospital lobbies. Mark areas that flood. Walk part of each route on a normal day so it feels familiar. Agree with your household which route you will use so they know where to look for you.

steps.title: Use the first 30 minutes to think
steps.body: When transit stops, many people rush out at once with little information. Unless you are in danger where you are, take 15-30 minutes to learn what happened. Check official alerts, transit agency updates, and local news. Is this a short delay or a long shutdown? Is it local or citywide? Is it safer to stay at work? Text your household and your out-of-area contact with your plan and route. Use the restroom, fill your water bottle, and change into walking shoes before you leave. A short pause often saves hours of walking the wrong way.

steps.title: Travel in a small group
steps.body: Walking with 2-4 coworkers who live in the same direction is safer and easier than going alone. Before leaving, agree on the route, the pace (set by the slowest person), and a rule for splitting off near each person's home. Pick one person to navigate. Share loads so no one is overloaded. Stop briefly every 45-60 minutes to drink water, check feet, and check in. Stay on main, busy streets. If anyone feels faint, has chest pain, or cannot keep going, stop and get help.

steps.title: Protect your feet
steps.body: Blisters can stop you long before you reach home. Wear broken-in walking shoes, never new shoes or heels, and socks that wick moisture rather than cotton. At the first warm or tender spot, stop and cover it with moleskin, tape, or a blister bandage before it becomes a blister. Carry dry socks and change them if your feet get wet. Air your feet for a few minutes at long rests. Anyone with diabetes or poor circulation should check their feet at every stop.

steps.title: Stay safe on the way
steps.body: Watch for dark traffic signals and treat them as all-way stops - drivers may not. Never wade through flooded streets; manholes and storm drains may be open under the water. Stay away from downed wires. Avoid shortcuts through alleys, rail yards, and empty underpasses. Drink water before you are thirsty, and in heat, rest in shade during the hottest hours. When you reach home, text your contact so everyone knows you made it.

warnings: Never walk through floodwater in city streets - open manholes and storm drains can be hidden under it.
Do not take shortcuts through isolated alleys, underpasses, or rail yards.
Do not walk on subway or rail tracks - they may be electrified and trains may still move.
Stop and get help if anyone has chest pain, confusion, or signs of heat illness.
proTips: A folding bike or scooter at work can turn a 5-hour walk into a 1-hour ride - if the roads are clear.
Keep a printed list of key phone numbers in your kit; you may need to borrow a phone.
Set your phone to low-power mode before you start walking.
Wear walking shoes on high-risk days; it costs nothing if nothing happens.

sources.title: Plan Now NYC - make an emergency plan
Driving Safely During a Power Outage

whenNotTo: Do not start walking if officials order people to shelter in place, during severe weather, or if staying at work is safer.
Do not attempt a walk that will put you outside after dark in dangerous conditions if you can stay put until morning.

quickGlance.situation: Trains and buses have stopped and you need to get home from work or school on foot.
immediate: Take 15-30 minutes to check official news and decide if staying put is safer
Text your household your route and plan
Change into walking shoes and fill your water
then: Walk your planned route with a small group at the slowest person's pace
Treat hot spots on your feet early and avoid floodwater and downed wires

title: High-Rise Fire - Stairwells, When to Stay, and Elevators
summary: What to do when the fire alarm sounds or you find fire in an apartment or office tower: when to get out by the stairs, when staying sealed in your unit is safer, and why the elevator is off-limits.

steps.title: Know your building before a fire
steps.body: Fire codes define a high-rise as a building over 75 feet (about 23 m) tall, roughly seven stories or more. These buildings take longer to evacuate, but they are more likely to have sprinklers, alarms, and voice announcements. Learn where every exit stair on your floor is in case the closest one fills with smoke. Ask management whether the building is sprinklered and whether it is fire-resistive ('fireproof') or not, and how emergency announcements work. Read the fire safety guide your building gives out. Keep exit stairs and stair doors clear, closed, and unlocked, and report problems.

steps.title: If the fire is in your unit, get out and close the door
steps.body: If the fire is in your own apartment or office, everyone leaves now - in any type of building. Stay low under smoke. Do not stop to fight a fire that is bigger than a wastebasket or to grab belongings. Close the door behind you as you leave. A closed door holds smoke and heat inside the unit; an open door lets them pour into halls and stairwells and can kill people floors away. Pull the fire alarm on your way out, knock on neighbors' doors on your floor, and call 911 from a safe spot with the exact address, floor, and unit.

steps.title: If the alarm sounds and the fire is elsewhere
steps.body: Listen to building announcements and follow fire department instructions - they know where the fire is. If you are told to stay, stay in your unit until firefighters reach you or say it is safe. If you are not told to stay, NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration advise leaving by the stairs. Before opening your door, feel it and the knob with the back of your hand. If it is hot, or smoke is pouring in around it, keep it shut and use the stay-in-place steps below. If it is cool, open it slowly, look for smoke, and go to the nearest clear stair.

steps.title: Use the stairs, never the elevator
steps.body: Do not use elevators during a fire unless the fire department directs you to. Elevators can stop at the fire floor, open into smoke, or lose power with you inside, and the shaft can fill with smoke. Walk down the stairs, holding the handrail, and keep to one side so firefighters can come up. If you meet heavy smoke in a stairwell, do not push through it - go back and try a different stair, or return to your unit and seal yourself in. Close stair doors behind you. Once outside, go to your meeting place, stay there, and tell firefighters if anyone may be trapped.

steps.title: Know when staying is safer
steps.body: The FDNY teaches that building type matters. In a non-fireproof building - most private homes, brownstones, and small older walk-ups - fire can spread unit to unit, so it is usually safer to leave right away. In a fire-resistive (fireproof) building, walls and floors are designed to hold fire where it starts, so if the fire is not in your unit and halls or stairs are smoky, staying in your sealed unit is often safer than walking into smoke. This is especially true when the fire is below you, because heat and smoke rise into stairwells. When in doubt, call 911 and ask.

steps.title: If you stay, seal the room and signal
steps.body: Keep your door closed. Stuff wet towels or sheets along the bottom and sides of the door and over vents, or tape the gaps. Turn off air conditioners and fans that pull in outside air. Call 911, give your apartment number and conditions, and stay on the line. Hang a bright cloth or wave a flashlight at a window so firefighters can find you. Unless smoke or flames are coming from below, you may open a window a few inches for fresh air, then close it if smoke enters. Never break windows - falling glass hurts people below and you cannot close a broken window against smoke.

steps.title: Plan for people who cannot use stairs
steps.body: People who use wheelchairs, have heart or lung disease, or cannot hear alarms need a plan before a fire. Tell building management and keep the fire department's access in mind. A good plan names helpers on your floor, picks the safest place to wait (often your own sealed unit in a fireproof building, or a designated area by a protected stair), and includes a phone to call 911 with your exact location. Practice it. Building staff evacuate too and may not reach everyone, so do not depend on them alone.

warnings: Never use the elevator in a fire unless firefighters direct you to.
Always close your apartment door behind you - an open door spreads deadly smoke through the building.
Do not walk into a smoke-filled stairwell; turn back and use another stair or shelter in a sealed room.
Never break windows - falling glass injures people below and you lose the ability to close out smoke.
proTips: Keep shoes, a headlamp, keys, and a phone by your bed - fires at night kill the most people.
Check whether your apartment door self-closes; if it does not, ask management to fix it.
Keep a roll of duct tape and a couple of old towels in a bathroom cabinet for sealing a door fast.
When you hear an alarm, start moving or sealing right away - do not wait to see smoke.

sources.title: State Fire Marshal Offers Safety Tips for High-Rise Dwellers (NFPA guidance)
FDNY offers safety guidance for fireproof and non-fireproof buildings

whenNotTo: Do not stay in place if the fire is in your own unit - get out and close the door.
Do not stay in place in a non-fireproof building when you can safely reach a clear exit.
Do not leave your unit into heavy smoke or past a hot door just because the alarm is sounding.

quickGlance.situation: The fire alarm is sounding or you see fire or smoke in an apartment or office tower.
immediate: If the fire is in your unit, get everyone out and close the door behind you
Feel your door before opening; if cool and clear, take the stairs - never the elevator
If the door is hot or halls are smoky, stay in, seal the door, and call 911
then: Follow building announcements and firefighter instructions
Go to your meeting place outside and report anyone trapped

title: Stuck in an Elevator, Subway, or Tunnel During an Outage
summary: What to do when the power fails and you are trapped in an elevator, a stopped subway or commuter train, or a road tunnel - and why climbing out on your own is usually the most dangerous choice.

steps.title: Elevator: stay calm and call for help
steps.body: When the power fails, an elevator stops by itself and its brakes hold it in place - cars do not free-fall. If the car is level with a floor, press 'Door Open' and step out carefully, watching for a gap or step. If not, press the alarm or help button and use the car's intercom or emergency phone. Tell the operator the building address and which elevator you are in. Responders often arrive within minutes, but in a citywide outage it can take much longer. Cars have vents, so you will not run out of air, even if it gets warm. Call or text someone outside if your phone works.

steps.title: Elevator: do not force doors or climb out
steps.body: Do not pry the doors open, crawl through a partly open door, or climb out the ceiling hatch. The car can move without warning when power returns, and people are seriously hurt or killed falling into the shaft. Only a trained elevator technician or firefighters should do a rescue. If you are outside a stuck elevator, do not try to rescue people yourself - call the elevator company or building management and tell them people are trapped, since entrapments get priority. Call 911 if anyone inside has a medical emergency, if there is smoke or fire, or if no one answers the alarm.

steps.title: Elevator: wait well
steps.body: Sit down, loosen tight clothing, and sip water if you have it. Bang on the door or call out every few minutes so people know you are still there. Use your phone light sparingly to save battery. Keep children close and talk calmly - panic makes waiting harder and spreads to others. If someone has a medical condition, tell the operator. Afterwards, think about whether you should use stairs during heat waves and storms when outages are more likely, especially if you rely on medicines or oxygen.

steps.title: Subway or train: stay on board
steps.body: Transit agencies like the MTA say the safest place during a train emergency is usually on the train. The tracks may still be electrified, and other trains may be moving nearby. Stay calm, stay seated, and listen for announcements. Tell the crew right away about any fire, smoke, or medical problem using the intercom near the doors if your car has one. If there is smoke or a problem in your car, walk calmly to the next car that is not affected - in most cases that is all you need to do. Do not pull the emergency brake unless the train's movement itself is putting lives in danger, and avoid pulling it in a tunnel.

steps.title: Subway or train: only leave with the crew
steps.body: Self-evacuating onto the tracks is one of the biggest risks in a stalled train. The third rail carries hundreds of volts and can kill instantly, and you may not see an oncoming train in a dark tunnel. Wait for the crew to guide you. Most evacuations are done by pulling a rescue train alongside or walking through to a station. If crews do lead you out, follow their directions exactly, watch your step, tell them if you need help, and stay away from the third rail and any wires. Only if your life is in immediate danger and no crew is coming should you use the emergency exit release shown on the door or window labels.

steps.title: Road tunnel: if there is fire or smoke
steps.body: Do not enter a tunnel if you see smoke at the entrance or your car is smoking. If a fire starts in the tunnel, pull over, turn off the engine, leave the key in the car, and get out right away - leave belongings behind. Call 911 or use a tunnel emergency phone. Use a tunnel fire extinguisher only on a very small fire if it is safe. Otherwise walk to the nearest marked emergency exit and leave the tunnel, helping others who need it. Smoke can fill a tunnel in minutes, so move away from it and do not wait in your car.

steps.title: Road tunnel: if traffic stops
steps.body: In stopped traffic, keep a safe gap from the car ahead, even when moving slowly. Turn on hazard lights and tune to the radio for tunnel or traffic updates. Note where emergency phones, extinguishers, and exits are. Follow instructions from tunnel staff and electronic signs. If the power goes out and lights fail, stay in your car with the engine off unless there is smoke or fire or staff tell you to leave, and use your headlights to see. Keep a flashlight in your car for exactly this situation.

warnings: Never pry open elevator doors or climb out of the car - the elevator can move without warning.
Do not leave a stalled train onto the tracks without the crew - the third rail and other trains can kill you.
In a road tunnel fire, leave your car and walk to an emergency exit - smoke moves fast.
Do not try to rescue people from an elevator yourself; call the elevator company or 911.
proTips: Carry a small flashlight and a water bottle in your daily bag - they make a long wait much easier.
When you board a train, glance at the emergency instruction stickers so you know where they are.
In a building with frequent outages, use the stairs during storms and heat waves.
Teach children that the elevator alarm button is how to call for help.
source: Otis / Southern California Edison / MTA / FHWA

sources.title: 5 steps to take if your elevator stops

whenNotTo: Do not stay in a road tunnel car when there is fire or smoke - get out and walk to an exit.
Do not stay in a train car that is filling with smoke - move to an unaffected car and alert the crew.

quickGlance.situation: The power fails while you are in an elevator, a subway or commuter train, or a road tunnel.
immediate: Elevator: press the alarm, use the intercom, and do not force the doors
Train: stay on board and tell the crew about smoke or injuries
Tunnel fire: engine off, key in, get out and walk to an emergency exit
then: Wait for trained responders or crew to lead you out
Call 911 for any fire, smoke, or medical emergency

title: Finding Help in a City After a Disaster - Shelters, FEMA Recovery Centers, Red Cross, and 211
summary: Where to go and who to call for a place to sleep, food, water, medical help, and money to recover after a disaster - and how to apply for FEMA help without getting scammed.

steps.title: Call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies
steps.body: Keep 911 free for fires, serious injuries, people trapped, and crimes in progress. For everything else - shelter locations, food, water, medical supplies, housing, and help paying bills - dial 211. 211 is a free, confidential service run by United Way partners in nearly every part of the U.S. It is answered 24/7 in many areas, offers interpreters in many languages, and can also be reached by text and online search in most states. During disasters, 211 centers share shelter locations, road closures, and public health notices so callers get current information and 911 lines stay open.

steps.title: Find an open shelter
steps.body: Listen to local officials first - if you are told to evacuate, they will direct you to an evacuation point where you get shelter information. You can also use the Red Cross 'Find an Open Shelter' map online or in Red Cross apps, check your city or county emergency management site, or call 211. Red Cross shelters are free and open to anyone with a disaster-related need. You do not need ID - just your name and where you lived before the disaster. Shelters are accessible to people with disabilities. Tell staff about medical equipment, diet, or religious needs. If no shelter shows up near you, check again later; sites open as needed.

steps.title: Know what shelters provide and what to bring
steps.body: Shelters offer a safe place to sleep, meals, snacks, water, and health help for disaster needs such as first aid, replacing lost prescriptions, and replacing lost glasses. They also offer emotional support and help reconnecting with family. Some also have caseworkers, childcare, and laundry. If you have time, bring bedding, clothing, medicines, your emergency kit, phone chargers, and a comfort item for each child. Do not bring alcohol, drugs, or weapons. Service animals are always welcome; pets may be housed at a separate site run by animal groups. Never delay leaving to pack - your safety comes first.

steps.title: Use day-time service sites and distribution points
steps.body: Not everyone needs a bed. After big disasters, the Red Cross and partners run service sites that offer meals, device charging, cleanup kits, health services, and caseworkers without overnight stays. Cities also open cooling or warming centers, water and food distribution points, and charging stations, often at libraries, schools, and community centers. Food banks and faith groups add more. 211 and local radio usually have the most current list. Bring your own containers for water and a bag for supplies.

steps.title: Apply for FEMA assistance
steps.body: FEMA individual help is only available after a major disaster is declared for your area. Apply online at DisasterAssistance.gov, in the free FEMA App, by phone at 1-800-621-3362 (open 24/7, with multilingual operators), or in person at a Disaster Recovery Center. Have ready: Social Security numbers, the damaged home's address, a description of the damage, insurance details, household income, a phone number and mailing address, and bank information for direct deposit. Photograph damage and list lost items first. You can apply before your insurance claim is settled. Save your 9-digit application number.

steps.title: Visit a Disaster Recovery Center
steps.body: After a declared disaster, FEMA and the state open Disaster Recovery Centers (DRCs) in or near hard-hit areas, sometimes in mobile units. Anyone can walk in - you do not need to have applied first. Staff help you apply for FEMA aid, upload documents, understand letters, and connect with other programs such as low-interest Small Business Administration disaster loans, which are also open to homeowners and renters. Find centers, hours, and services with the FEMA DRC Locator or the FEMA App, or by texting 'DRC' and your ZIP code to 43362.

steps.title: Protect yourself from scams
steps.body: Disasters bring scammers. FEMA and SBA never charge a fee to apply for help. Real FEMA inspectors carry official photo ID and will already have your application number - they will not ask you for bank PINs or passwords. Do not pay anyone who promises to speed up your claim. Hire only licensed, insured contractors and never pay in full up front. Donate only to charities you know. If you are denied, read the letter; it explains how to appeal, and many denials are fixed by sending a missing document.

warnings: Do not delay evacuation to pack for a shelter - leave when told to.
FEMA and SBA never charge to apply - anyone asking for a fee is a scammer.
Do not bring weapons, alcohol, or drugs to a shelter.
Keep 911 for life-threatening emergencies so it stays open for people who need it.
proTips: Write 211 and 1-800-621-3362 on your family emergency card in case your phone dies.
Keep phone photos of your ID, insurance cards, and lease or deed so you can apply even if papers are lost.
Go to a DRC early in the day and bring a charger, water, and snacks - lines can be long.
Keep a notebook of every call: date, name, and what you were told.

sources.title: How do I apply for FEMA assistance?

whenNotTo: Do not call 211 for an emergency in progress - call 911.
Do not travel to a shelter through floodwater or active danger; wait for officials or call 911 for rescue.

quickGlance.situation: A disaster has damaged your home or cut off services and you need shelter, supplies, or recovery money.
immediate: Call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies; dial 211 for shelters, food, and water
Check the Red Cross shelter map or local officials for open shelters - no ID needed
Photograph damage before cleaning up
then: Apply for FEMA help at DisasterAssistance.gov, the FEMA App, or 1-800-621-3362
Visit a Disaster Recovery Center and never pay anyone to apply

title: Scavenging and Salvage - What Is Legal, Ethical, and Safe
summary: How to tell legal salvage from looting after a disaster, how to salvage your own property and accepted items safely, and the hidden hazards - sharp debris, asbestos, lead, mold, and unstable buildings - that injure people doing it.

steps.title: Know the line between salvage and looting
steps.body: Taking property from inside someone else's home, store, shed, garage, or porch without permission is theft or burglary, and many states punish looting during a declared emergency more harshly than normal theft. 'Abandoned' does not mean 'free' - owners who evacuated still own everything they left behind, including damaged items. Police patrol disaster zones closely and may arrest people found inside damaged buildings or carrying goods away. Curfews may also make it illegal to be out at all. Unless you are in a true life-or-death emergency and have no other option, take only what is yours or what the owner has clearly given you.

steps.title: Check the local rules on curbside debris
steps.body: Rules for debris piles at the curb differ from city to city. After a recent hurricane, St. Petersburg, Florida police said taking items from curbside piles was not looting, while Rowlett, Texas passed an ordinance after its tornado making it a misdemeanor to sort through or take items from someone's curb without permission. Many other towns have similar 'no scavenging' rules, partly because thieves claim stolen goods came from the curb. Before you take anything, check your city's notices or ask a police officer. Even where it is legal, ask the owner if they are there - watching strangers pick through your belongings is painful after a disaster.

steps.title: Salvage the right things - your own first
steps.body: Focus on your own home and on items owners offer to you. Before moving anything, photograph damage for insurance and FEMA. High-value salvage after a disaster is usually not food: it is tarps, lumber for patching, tools, clean containers, bedding that stayed dry, and documents. Throw away any food, water, medicine, baby bottles, or cosmetics that touched floodwater, unless they were in sealed metal cans you can clean and disinfect. Throw out food from fridges and freezers that warmed above safe temperatures. Never salvage gas cans, propane tanks, or chemical containers from debris - leave them for hazardous-waste crews.

steps.title: Wear the right protection
steps.body: Debris injures more people than the disaster in some cleanups. Wear sturdy boots with thick soles (waterproof if there was flooding), heavy work gloves, long sleeves and pants, safety glasses or goggles, and a hard hat around damaged structures. Wear a well-fitted N95 respirator for dust and mold; note that a dust mask does not protect against fuel or chemical vapors. Wash your hands and any skin that touched debris or floodwater with soap and clean water. Get a tetanus shot if you have not had one in 10 years, and see a health provider for deep or dirty wounds and puncture wounds.

steps.title: Stay out of unsafe buildings
steps.body: Do not enter a building with visible damage - sagging roofs, cracked walls, shifted foundations, or floors that feel soft - until an inspector or official says it is safe. Leave right away if you smell gas or hear creaking or shifting. Stay clear of downed power lines and do not touch anything in standing water that may be energized. Watch for nails, broken glass, and sharp metal hidden under water and mud. Snakes, rats, and stinging insects move into debris piles, so lift items with a tool, not your hands. Work with a partner who can call for help.

steps.title: Respect asbestos, lead, and mold
steps.body: Older buildings may contain asbestos in insulation, floor tiles, and siding, and lead in paint built before 1978. Breaking, sanding, or tearing these materials releases dust you should not breathe. Do not cut, sand, or tear out materials you suspect contain asbestos - removal must be done by trained, licensed contractors. Mist dusty debris lightly with water to keep dust down. Mold grows within a day or two in wet buildings; do not mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners, and wear gear before using any mold or germ killers. Call a professional for large or complex jobs.

steps.title: Help instead of take
steps.body: In a city recovery, the most useful scavenging is often sharing. Offer extra tools, tarps, and labor to neighbors. Work through organized volunteer cleanups run by local governments, faith groups, and established relief groups, which provide safety gear and know the rules. Report suspected looting to police rather than confronting people. Keeping your community's trust matters for months after the disaster - people remember who helped and who took.

warnings: Taking property from damaged homes or businesses is theft and can bring heavier penalties during a declared emergency.
Do not enter damaged buildings until officials say they are safe - collapse and gas leaks kill people during cleanup.
Do not disturb suspected asbestos or old lead paint - leave it to licensed professionals.
Throw out food, water, and medicine that touched floodwater unless sealed in cans you can clean.
proTips: Ask before you take - a quick 'Do you mind if I take this?' avoids misunderstandings and legal trouble.
Carry a pry bar or rake to lift debris; never reach under piles with your hands.
Keep a small kit of gloves, N95 masks, and safety glasses in your car for post-storm work.
Photograph your own items before moving them so insurance and FEMA claims hold up.
source: NJ Department of Health / local police and city notices

sources.title: Health officials urge caution during storm cleanup
New ordinance protects curbside debris in tornado-stricken Rowlett
How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

whenNotTo: Do not salvage during a curfew or in areas police have closed.
Do not salvage inside a damaged building that has not been cleared as safe.
Do not take anything from homes, stores, or enclosed areas without the owner's permission.

quickGlance.situation: After a disaster you want to recover useful items from debris - your own or someone else's.
immediate: Take only your own items or things the owner clearly gives you
Check local rules - curbside picking is legal in some cities and a crime in others
Wear boots, heavy gloves, eye protection, and an N95
then: Stay out of damaged buildings and leave asbestos and chemicals to professionals
Wash up after handling debris and get medical care for deep or dirty wounds

title: Balcony, Rooftop, and Windowsill Food Growing
summary: How to grow real food in containers on a balcony, rooftop, or sunny windowsill - choosing crops, pots, and potting mix, watering and feeding, and staying within your building's weight and safety limits.

steps.title: Check the rules and the weight limit first
steps.body: Ask your landlord, property manager, or HOA about balcony and roof garden rules before buying anything. Balconies have a maximum load, and wet soil is heavy - a large pot of wet garden soil can weigh well over 100 pounds (45 kg). Use lightweight potting mix, place heavy pots near the wall or over support beams rather than at the outer edge, and never put large containers on a roof without the building's approval. Keep pots away from railings where wind can knock them off, and never block a fire escape, exit, or firefighter access.

steps.title: Map your sun
steps.body: Sun decides what you can grow. For one day, note how many hours of direct sun each spot gets. Fruiting crops like tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant need at least 6 hours of direct sun. Lettuce, kale, spinach, chard, and many herbs tolerate partial shade (3-5 hours). South- and west-facing balconies are usually the sunniest in the U.S.; north-facing ones suit greens and herbs. Windowsills work well for herbs, microgreens, and green onions. High balconies are windier, which dries plants out faster, so use a wind screen or choose short, sturdy plants.

steps.title: Pick containers that are big enough
steps.body: Small pots dry out fast and stunt plants. Penn State Extension suggests pots at least 20 inches (50 cm) wide for tomatoes and about 14 inches (35 cm) for peppers and eggplant; herbs and greens can grow in smaller pots, window boxes, or long troughs. Pots should be at least as deep as they are wide. Every container needs drainage holes. Fabric grow bags, food-grade buckets with holes drilled in the bottom, and plastic tubs all work. Use saucers so water does not drip onto the balcony below - drips cause neighbor complaints and stains.

steps.title: Use potting mix, not garden soil
steps.body: Fill containers with a soilless potting mix made from materials like peat moss, coconut coir, bark, perlite, or vermiculite. Garden soil packs down in pots, drains poorly, and is much heavier. You can mix in up to about half compost for nutrients. Mix in a slow-release fertilizer at planting, then feed every 2-4 weeks with a water-soluble fertilizer following the label, since plants in pots can only use the nutrients in their small amount of soil. Refresh or replace the mix each season.

steps.title: Choose compact, productive crops
steps.body: Look for varieties labeled 'bush', 'compact', 'patio', or 'determinate'. Good container crops include cherry and patio tomatoes, peppers, bush beans, leaf lettuce, kale, chard, spinach, radishes, green onions, and herbs like basil, parsley, and mint (give mint its own pot - it spreads). Pole beans, cucumbers, and vining tomatoes can grow up a trellis to save space. Skip sweet corn, watermelon, winter squash, and zucchini - they need more room than a balcony gives. Sow fast crops like radishes and lettuce every 2-3 weeks for a steady supply.

steps.title: Water deeply and often
steps.body: Containers dry out much faster than garden beds. In hot summer weather, most container vegetables need watering at least once a day, and small pots on windy balconies may need it twice. Push a finger 1 inch (2.5 cm) into the mix; if it is dry, water slowly until water runs out the bottom. Keep the mix moist but not soggy. Mulch the top with straw or bark to slow drying. Collect rainwater if your building allows it, and in a water outage reuse clean rinse water from washing vegetables - never use greywater with soap or bleach on edible plants.

steps.title: Set realistic expectations
steps.body: A balcony garden will not feed a family on its own, but it can add fresh greens, herbs, and vitamins to a stored-food diet and lift morale in a long emergency. A few pots of greens can give a salad several times a week. Start small - 4 to 6 pots - and learn what works in your spot before expanding. Save seeds from open-pollinated varieties to replant. Keep a small stock of seeds, potting mix, and fertilizer in storage so you can start growing even if stores are closed.

warnings: Check your balcony's load limit and building rules - wet soil is very heavy.
Keep pots away from railings and never block fire escapes or exits.
Do not water edible plants with greywater that contains soap, bleach, or chemicals.
Do not use garden soil in containers - it is heavy and drains poorly.
proTips: A 5-gallon food-grade bucket with drainage holes grows one tomato or pepper plant well.
Self-watering containers with a water reservoir cut daily watering on hot balconies.
Herbs on a sunny kitchen windowsill are the easiest first garden.
Grow microgreens indoors on a tray - they are ready to eat in 1-3 weeks.
source: Penn State Extension / Alameda County Library

sources.title: Container Vegetable Gardening: Four Keys to Success
Balcony Gardening: Before You Get Started

whenNotTo: Do not place heavy planters on a balcony or roof that shows cracks, rust, or sagging - get it inspected first.
Do not count on a container garden as your main food source in an emergency.

quickGlance.situation: You live in an apartment or city home and want to grow some of your own food in limited space.
immediate: Check building rules and keep heavy pots near the wall, away from railings
Find spots with at least 6 hours of sun for fruiting crops
Use large pots with drainage holes and light potting mix
then: Plant compact greens, herbs, and patio tomatoes; water daily in summer
Feed every 2-4 weeks and replant fast crops every few weeks

title: Getting Out of a City - When to Leave, Timing, and Routes on Foot and by Car
summary: How to decide when leaving the city beats staying, why leaving early matters more than any route trick, and how to get out by car or on foot without getting trapped in traffic or danger.

steps.title: Decide: stay or go
steps.body: For most city emergencies - outages, storms, unrest a few blocks away - staying home is safer than joining a mass exodus. Leave when officials order an evacuation, when a known threat such as a hurricane, wildfire, flood, or chemical release is heading for your area, or when your home becomes unsafe or unlivable (no water, heat, or cooling for vulnerable family members). Many places use two levels: an evacuation warning means get ready and leave now if you need extra time, and an evacuation order means leave now. If you would need help to leave, go at the warning.

steps.title: Leave early
steps.body: Ready.gov advises leaving early enough that you are not trapped by severe weather. Timing beats every route trick: the first hours of a large evacuation move far faster than later ones, when roads clog, gas stations run dry, and bridges close. Do not wait to see how bad it gets. Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times and fill up when evacuation seems likely - stations may close or lose power. Take one car per family to cut congestion. If you have no car, arrange a ride now with family, friends, or your city's evacuation assistance program.

steps.title: Plan destinations in more than one direction
steps.body: Pick at least three places you could go - a relative, friend, hotel, or shelter - in different directions from the city. The threat decides which way you can go: away from the coast for a hurricane, upwind for a chemical release or wildfire, uphill for flooding. Tell your out-of-area contact where you are heading. Save offline maps and carry a paper road map. Know where shelters and evacuation points are, and check that your destination will take your pets - public shelters may admit only service animals.

steps.title: Drive the official routes
steps.body: Follow the evacuation routes officials give. Shortcuts and back roads can be blocked, flooded, or closed, and you may not be able to turn around. Listen to a battery radio for updates. Watch for washed-out roads and bridges and downed power lines. Never drive into floodwater - just 12 inches (30 cm) of moving water can float many cars. Treat dark traffic signals as all-way stops. Drive with headlights on, keep calm in heavy traffic, and keep the tank above a quarter if you can. Carry water, snacks, medicines, chargers, and a full go-bag in the car.

steps.title: Leave on foot if you must
steps.body: If roads are gridlocked or you have no car, walking or biking may be faster. Wear sturdy shoes, long pants and sleeves, and a hat. Carry water, food, medicines, a light, a phone and power bank, a paper map, and copies of key documents. Use sidewalks and pedestrian bridges, not highway lanes or rail tracks. Travel with others when you can, and stop for water and foot care every hour. In heat or smoke, move during cooler hours and wear an N95 for smoke. Head for the evacuation point or shelter officials name - buses often run from there.

steps.title: Before you lock the door
steps.body: If you have time: text your out-of-area contact your route and destination, check if neighbors need a ride, and leave a note saying when you left and where you went. Lock doors and windows. Unplug small electronics, but leave the fridge and freezer on unless flooding is expected. Shut off water, gas, or electricity only if officials tell you to or your home is damaged - turning gas back on requires a professional. Bring pets with their food, leash, and carrier. Do not delay leaving to pack more.

steps.title: Do not return too soon
steps.body: Stay away until officials say it is safe to return. Roads may be damaged, power lines down, and buildings unsafe. When you go back, enter in daylight, watch for gas smells and structural damage, and photograph everything before cleanup. Expect checkpoints; carry ID and proof of address so you can get back into your neighborhood.

warnings: Never drive into floodwater - a foot of moving water can float many cars.
Do not take shortcuts around official evacuation routes; they may be blocked or flooded.
Do not wait until roads are jammed - leaving early is the single most important choice.
Do not walk on highways or rail lines when leaving on foot.
proTips: Keep the gas tank above half all the time in hurricane and wildfire seasons.
Pack the car the night a warning is issued so you can leave in minutes.
Write your three destinations and routes on a card in the glovebox.
Put a printed contact list and copies of IDs in a sealed bag in your go-bag.
source: FEMA Ready.gov / NYC Emergency Management / Boulder ODM

sources.title: Driving Safely During a Power Outage

whenNotTo: Do not evacuate into the path of a storm, fire, or flood when officials say sheltering in place is safer.
Do not leave during a shelter-in-place order for a chemical or radiological release unless officials tell you to.

quickGlance.situation: A threat is heading for your city or officials are warning people to evacuate.
immediate: Leave at the warning stage, not when roads are already jammed
Fill the gas tank and load your go-bag, medicines, and pets
Follow official routes - no shortcuts, no floodwater
then: Text your out-of-area contact your route and destination
Stay away until officials say it is safe to return
